hook: Compress a whole report into one paragraph, and keep yourself out of it.
intro: Summarising is among the most useful things you can do in writing, and among the easiest to do badly. Two failures are common: smuggling your own view in, and nominalising so hard the paragraph stops breathing. Write 900 to 1800 characters. Keep every claim attributed, keep yourself invisible, and nominalise only where it genuinely tightens the sentence. The correction will check both: whether anything in your summary was not in the source, and whether the nominal style has made a sentence that no one could read aloud.
tips[0].title: Attribute everything, claim nothing
tips[0].text: A summary reports what someone else said. Keep the source in the sentence, with a verb of saying or a source phrase, and the reader can never mistake the claim for yours. Where the writing gets dense, the Konjunktiv I carries the attribution on its own.
tips[0].check.why: Konjunktiv I keeps it his claim rather than the summary’s own.
tips[0].trap: One indicative sentence in the middle hands the author’s claim to you.
tips[1].title: Nominalise to tighten, not to impress
tips[1].text: Turning a verb into a noun lets one sentence hold what took two: die Senkung der Kosten, der Rückgang der Nachfrage, nach Einführung der Regel. It earns its place when it shortens. When three genitives chain together, turn one back into a verb.
tips[1].check.why: One nominalisation tightens; four in a row stop the sentence working.
tips[2].title: Four moves and nothing else
tips[2].text: Subject, central claim, evidence, conclusion. A summary that adds a fifth move is reviewing, and a summary that drops the evidence is a headline. Your own judgement belongs to a different text.
tips[2].check.why: That is a review. A summary reports and stops.
tips[2].visual.moves[0].label: Source
tips[2].visual.moves[1].label: Main claim
tips[2].visual.moves[2].label: Evidence
tips[2].visual.moves[3].label: Conclusion
remember[0]: Name the text, the subject and the central claim in sentence one.
remember[1]: Attribute every claim; Konjunktiv I carries it where the writing is dense.
remember[2]: Nominalise where it shortens; unpick the third genitive in a chain.
remember[3]: Subject, claim, evidence, conclusion, and nothing of your own.
exam: Summarising a written source is the task C1 writing is built on, and the one skill every German office job quietly assumes.
mistakes[0].why: Konjunktiv I for the claim, and your own agreement has no place.
mistakes[1].why: A genitive chain that long has to be unpicked back into verbs.
mistakes[2].why: A summary reports the content, not your impression of it.
mistakes[3].why: No comma, and the verb takes second place after the source phrase.
tips[2].check.q: What does not belong in a summary?
tips[2].check.options[0]: whether you found the argument convincing
tips[2].check.answer: whether you found the argument convincing
